rationale: The strongest alternative—remote coastlands and their Gentile populations—fits the cited occurrences more directly and with fewer unsupported transitions. Genesis 10:5 identifies ethnolinguistically divided Gentile territories; Isaiah 11:11 treats the islands as places from which God recovers his remnant, distinguishing the islands from the recovered people; and Isaiah 42:4 and 51:5 naturally portray distant peoples awaiting God’s law and salvation. These texts do not establish that an island specifically signifies a holy covenant community extracted from a symbolic sea. Revelation 16:20 says that every island fled during cosmic judgment, but it neither identifies the islands as faithful people nor says their flight is preservation. Thus the entry combines several suggestive motifs into a definition that the cited evidence does not carry better than the established coastlands/distant-nations reading.
book_core_identification: An island represents a holy or covenantally set-apart people distinguished from the surrounding mass of nations.
book_secondary_elaborations: The set-apart people rises from the sea of nations.
The people waits for God’s law.
The people is preserved while surrounding kingdoms fall.
unsupported_glossary_assertions: That islands specifically represent a holy or covenantally set-apart people rather than distant or geographically distinguished peoples generally.
That islands rise from a symbolic sea of nations.
That the flight of every island in Revelation 16:20 means preservation while surrounding kingdoms fall.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter’s claim that Hebrew iy has a uniform symbolic usage is weakened by plainly geographical and ethnographic occurrences.
The derivation of an island from the combined meanings of sea, mountain, and rock is conceptually ingenious but is not an explicit scriptural identification.
The appeal to Job 22:30 as “the island of the innocent” depends on the KJV rendering of a text commonly parsed and translated without any reference to an island.

The chapter’s claim that there are no islands in the new creation because nothing remains to be set apart from is not asserted in the glossary entry and is not independently established by Revelation 21:1.
strongest_counter_interpretation: “Isles” ordinarily denotes literal or representative remote coastlands and their populations, especially distant Gentile nations or the ends of the inhabited world. In Isaiah these distant peoples are summoned to hear, await, and receive God’s rule; in Revelation islands function with mountains as parts of the world displaced or removed in cosmic judgment, without necessarily carrying Isaiah’s missionary sense.
counter_core_identification: Remote coastlands and their Gentile peoples, not specifically a preserved covenant community separated from a symbolic sea.
material_core_denial: The term’s representative force is geographical and ethnographic—remote peoples—not an encoded identification of islands with holy communities extracted from humanity.
counter_case: Genesis 10:5 explicitly calls them “isles of the Gentiles” divided by lands, languages, families, and nations, supporting maritime peoples or territories rather than a faithful remnant.
Isaiah 11:11 says the remnant is recovered “from” the islands, grammatically distinguishing the remnant from the islands that contain it.
Isaiah 42:4 and 51:5 readily describe distant peoples awaiting God’s law and salvation; awaiting salvation does not itself mean they already constitute a sanctified, set-apart people.
Revelation 16:20 pairs islands with mountains in universal upheaval. Nothing in the excerpt identifies fleeing with rescue or contrasts preserved believers with fallen kingdoms.
The common reading accommodates both literal geography and prophetic representation without requiring the unstated equation island = covenant ground.
book_explanatory_advantages: It integrates the island image with the supplied chapter’s well-supported identification of waters as peoples and nations.
It notices that Genesis 10:5 presents island peoples as differentiated rather than undifferentiated.
It unifies the Isaiah passages’ repeated portrayal of the isles as responsive to God’s law, righteousness, and salvation.
It attempts to explain the different verbs applied to islands and mountains in Revelation 16:20.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It follows the ordinary lexical sense of islands or coastlands and the explicit ethnogeographic language of Genesis 10:5.
It explains why Isaiah repeatedly addresses the isles alongside distant peoples and nations.
It preserves the distinction in Isaiah 11:11 between the remnant and the islands from which that remnant is recovered.
It reads Revelation 16:20 within its immediate cosmic-judgment pairing without importing an unstated rescue scenario.
It does not require island, sea, mountain, and rock to retain fixed compositional symbolic values across unrelated contexts.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Isaiah 11:11 locates the remnant in and recovers it from the islands, rather than identifying the islands themselves as the remnant or set-apart people.
Genesis 10:5 applies “isles” broadly to divided Gentile lands and nations without identifying them as covenantally holy.
Revelation 16:20 says every island fled, but supplies no indication that the flight is preservation; the universal wording instead belongs naturally to the dissolution of the present world order.
unresolved_objections: The Isaiah passages do allow distant Gentile peoples to become responsive to God and therefore potentially set apart; the book’s theme is possible as a theological development, though not established as the term’s defining symbolism.

The contrast between islands fleeing and mountains not being found in Revelation 16:20 may be meaningful, but the supplied text does not determine that it means rescue rather than two descriptions of cosmic removal.
